messages.content:
You are a clinical psychologist writing a psychological case vignette
grounded in Ehlers & Clark's (2000) cognitive model of PTSD.

Write a realistic clinical case vignette for a patient with PTSD.
The vignette should read as a cohesive, flowing portrait — not a structured report.
Weave together who this person is, what happened to them, how they experience their
symptoms day to day, how they cope, and what toll this takes on their life and relationships.


Do not use section headers, numbered points, or clinical labels for symptoms.
Write 200–300 words in third person.
Cover: presenting complaints, trauma background, cognitive distortions, avoidance, and maintaining factors.
Avoid excessive jargon - write for a clinical case conference audience.

Please write a clinical vignette for the following patient presenting with PTSD.
Patient demographics:
- Age: 52
- Gender: Male
- Ethnicity: European
- Relationship Status: In a relationship
- Occupation: Film Director
- Trauma Type: Life-threatening accident
- Pcl5: 35

The first thing I noticed about him was the way he looked at the empty space in front of him. Not at me, not at the window, but at a point about three feet in front of his face, as if he was watching a scene play out on an invisible screen. He is a film director, so I initially dismissed it as habit—the way a visual storyteller frames a shot in his mind. But as he began to speak, I realized he wasn't composing. He was trapped in a loop.

He tells me the accident happened eighteen months ago, on a Tuesday afternoon in late October. He was on location in a remote part of the Pacific Northwest, scouting for a nature documentary he was directing. The road was a narrow, winding logging track, slick with wet leaves. He remembers the exact sound of the tires losing grip—a low, wet hiss that he now hears in his sleep. The SUV slid sideways, rolled twice, and came to rest against a Douglas fir, its roof crushed down to the level of the steering wheel.

He was wearing his seatbelt. That single fact, he says, is the only reason he is alive. He hung upside down for forty-seven minutes before a hiker found him. He knows it was forty-seven minutes because he counted. He counted the seconds, then the minutes, then the beats of his own heart. He was not afraid, he tells me, not at first. He was lucid. He was thinking about the shot list for the next day. He was thinking about how the light would look through the shattered windshield at that angle. He was thinking about his partner, Lena, and whether she had remembered to buy milk.

Then the fear came. Not as a wave, but as a slow, cold crystallization in his chest. He realized he could not move his legs. He realized the fuel tank was leaking. He realized he was going to die.

The rescue was textbook. The hospital stay was brief—a concussion, three cracked ribs, a fractured scapula. No permanent damage. He was back at work six weeks later, directing a commercial for a luxury car brand. Everyone told him he was lucky. He agreed. He still agrees.

But the invisible screen is always there now. He sees the dashboard tilt, the green canopy of trees spinning, the dirt and gravel rushing up to meet him. It happens when he is driving, obviously, but also when he is standing in line at the grocery store, or sitting in a darkened editing bay, or lying in bed next to Lena. The loop plays without warning. He has learned to brace for it, but he cannot stop it.

He has become obsessive about time. He wears two watches—one analog, one digital—and checks them constantly. He arrives everywhere forty minutes early. He cannot tolerate a clock that is even a minute slow. He told me, with a thin, embarrassed smile, that he now times his showers. He times his meals. He times the silence between Lena’s words. He is not sure what he is measuring, only that he is terrified of losing track of it again.

His relationship with Lena is strained. She wants to help, but he cannot explain what he needs. He feels a constant, low-grade irritability, a static under his skin. He snaps at her for small things—a door left open, a glass placed too close to the edge of the table. He has stopped going to the movies. He cannot sit in the dark, in a room full of strangers, and let a story carry him away. He needs to be in control of the frame.

He came to me because he cannot direct anymore. He can do the technical work—the blocking, the lighting, the scheduling—but the creative spark is gone. He sits in the director’s chair and sees the scene, but he cannot feel it. He is a man watching his own life from a great distance, waiting for the next roll of the car.
